Stir into batters and energy bites for a protein boost.
Start with a small amount; the earthy flavor builds quickly.

hemp_protein.description: Protein-rich powder and hulled seeds ('hemp hearts') from Cannabis sativa cultivated for non-psychoactive food use. Hemp delivers a rare plant-based ratio of omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acids (~3:1) plus edestin and albumin proteins that are highly digestible. Nutty, grassy flavor reads best in smoothies, energy bars, granolas, and pesto bases. Unlike flax or chia, hemp hearts are soft enough to eat raw with no grinding required.

preparationTips: Best for marinating
Ideal for baking

pea_protein.name: pea_protein

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

flavorProfile.notes: Yellow-pea protein with a fairly neutral, mildly savory flavor; the base of many meat substitutes.

preparationTips: Blend into smoothies and shakes for a clean protein boost.
Whisk thoroughly — pea protein can clump in cold liquid.
Pair with cocoa or fruit to mask any faint earthy note.

pea_protein.description: Isolated protein fraction extracted from yellow split peas (Pisum sativum) via wet fractionation or dry milling. Neutral-flavored, allergen-friendly (soy-free, gluten-free, dairy-free), and high in BCAAs, it is the backbone of most modern plant-based burgers, sausages, and protein drinks. Forms gels on heating, emulsifies fats, and extrudes into fibrous meat-analog textures. Best hydrated with a touch of acid or salt to tame mild legume-earthiness.

preparationTips: Best for marinating
Ideal for baking

chickpea_protein.name: chickpea_protein

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

flavorProfile.notes: Chickpea-based protein with a gentle, nutty, legume flavor.

preparationTips: Whisk into batters; chickpea flour also sets into a savory pancake.
Blend into smoothies for a mild, nutty protein boost.
Cook chickpea-flour batters fully — raw, they taste bitter.

chickpea_protein.description: Protein-forward flour and isolate derived from Cicer arietinum — the garbanzo bean domesticated in southeastern Anatolia ~9,500 years ago. Besan (gram flour) is central to South Asian pakoras, socca/farinata of Nice and Liguria, and Provençal panisse; the cooking liquid (aquafaba) whips into stable vegan meringues. Delivers ~20g protein per 100g dry with a rich nutty-legume flavor that fries and bakes into firm, satisfying textures.

preparationTips: Best for marinating
Ideal for baking

lupin_protein.name: lupin_protein

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

flavorProfile.notes: High-protein lupin-bean flour or flakes with a mild, nutty taste.

preparationTips: Use de-bittered (sweet) lupin — bitter varieties need long soaking.
Blend the flour into batters and breads for extra protein.
It is a legume — treat it with care around peanut allergies.

lupin_protein.description: Ultra-high-protein legume (~40% dry protein) from sweet-cultivar Lupinus angustifolius or L. albus, traditionally brined as Mediterranean 'lupini' bean snacks and increasingly milled into flour for gluten-free pastas and meat analogs. Among the most sustainable crops on record — nitrogen-fixing, low-water, and cold-tolerant. Bitter wild varieties contain alkaloids; only sweet cultivars or thoroughly de-bittered beans are food-safe. Allergenic for some (cross-reacts with peanut).

preparationTips: Best for marinating
Ideal for baking

fava_protein.name: fava_protein

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

flavorProfile.notes: Fava-bean protein with an earthy, slightly green, legume flavor.

preparationTips: Blend into smoothies; pair with fruit to soften the earthy note.
Whisk into batters for a protein lift.
Treat it as a legume — note it around legume allergies.

fava_protein.description: Broad beans (Vicia faba), one of the oldest cultivated legumes — found in Neolithic deposits across the Mediterranean and Nile Valley. Fresh green favas dominate Italian springtime menus (crudo with pecorino); dried and split favas build Egyptian 'ful medames', Sicilian 'maccu', and Portuguese 'favada'. Rare warning: individuals with G6PD deficiency may develop favism, an acute hemolytic reaction to raw or undercooked fava consumption.

safetyThresholds.notes: Favism — individuals with G6PD deficiency (common in Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern, South Asian populations) can develop acute hemolytic anemia from raw, lightly cooked, or even pollen exposure. Cook thoroughly and know family medical history.

preparationTips: Best for marinating
Ideal for baking

moroccan.name: bessara
moroccan.preparation: pureed with olive oil and spices

flax_seeds.name: flax seeds

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

dried.temperature: refrigerator if ground; pantry if whole

flax_seeds.description: Tiny brown or golden seeds of *Linum usitatissimum*, exceptionally rich in alpha-linolenic acid (plant omega-3), lignans, and soluble fiber. Whole seeds pass through largely undigested — grind just before use to access their nutrients. Mixed with water, ground flax forms a gel ('flax egg') that binds vegan baked goods.

flavorProfile.notes: Grind in a spice grinder right before use; oils oxidize quickly.

preparationTips: 1 tbsp ground + 3 tbsp water = vegan egg substitute.
Refrigerate ground meal to prevent rancidity.

hemp_hearts.name: hemp hearts

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

hemp_hearts.description: Shelled seeds of *Cannabis sativa* (industrial hemp, non-psychoactive). Soft, slightly nutty seeds with a notable 10g protein per 3 tbsp serving and a near-ideal 3:1 omega-6:omega-3 ratio. Eaten raw on yogurt, salads, smoothies; no grinding required for digestion.

flavorProfile.notes: Eat raw or sprinkle over finished dishes — heat dulls the omega-3 oils.

preparationTips: Stir into smoothies for a protein boost.
Blend with water for a fast 'hemp milk'.

beef.name: Beef

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.container: Vacuum-sealed or wrapped tightly in butcher paper on a rimmed tray
storage.duration: 3–5 days fresh; up to 12 months frozen (vacuum-sealed)
storage.notes: Dry-aged beef stores dry, uncovered, in a dedicated chamber at 1–3°C and 80–85% humidity.

beef.description: Meat from domesticated cattle (*Bos taurus*), the foundation of protein-heavy cuisine across the Americas, Europe, and expanding globally. Flavor and texture vary dramatically by cut, breed, age, diet, and aging. Grass-finished beef has a yellower fat and more mineral, slightly gamey flavor; grain-finished is sweeter and more marbled. Dry-aging (21–60 days) concentrates flavor and tenderizes via enzymatic action. Primal cuts divide into tender quick-cook muscles (loin, rib) and harder-working cuts (chuck, brisket, shank) that reward long moist heat.

ribeye.name: Ribeye
ribeye.characteristics: Heavily marbled cut from the rib primal, with the spinalis dorsi 'ribeye cap' as its highlight.
ribeye.uses: Grilling, pan-searing at high heat; eats beautifully medium-rare.

strip.name: Strip / New York Strip
strip.characteristics: Tender, leaner cut from the short loin with a firm bite and beefy flavor.

tenderloin.name: Tenderloin / Filet Mignon
tenderloin.characteristics: Smallest, most tender cut; mild flavor, buttery texture.

chuck.name: Chuck
chuck.characteristics: Hard-working shoulder muscle with abundant connective tissue and rich flavor.
chuck.uses: Pot roast, short ribs, ground for burgers, slow braises.

brisket.name: Brisket
brisket.characteristics: Long, fibrous, heavily marbled pectoral muscle that transforms under long low heat.
brisket.uses: Barbecue smoking, corned beef, pastrami, pot au feu.

skirt.name: Skirt / Hanger / Flank
skirt.characteristics: Thin, loose-grained cuts from the plate and abdominals; intense flavor.
skirt.uses: Fajitas, carne asada, steak frites — slice across the grain.

wagyu.name: Wagyu
wagyu.characteristics: Japanese breeds (Kobe, Matsusaka) with extreme intramuscular marbling (BMS 8–12).
wagyu.uses: Quick sear, thin slice, small portions — the fat itself is the point.

flavorProfile.notes: Aging, breed, and feed drive enormous flavor differences before you ever season it.

preparationTips: Salt generously 45+ minutes ahead (or 15 minutes is worse than zero) to avoid surface moisture.
Tender cuts: high heat, short time; tough cuts: low heat, long time.
Always rest 5–10 min per inch of thickness.
Slice against the grain — grain direction matters more than knife skill.

toAvoid: delicate floral herbs on heavy braises

fresh.storage: Sealed on a tray, coldest part of the fridge (≤2°C).
tips: Bring steaks to room temperature 30–60 min before cooking.
Pat bone-dry before seasoning.
Don't move it until it releases from the pan.

safetyThresholds.notes: Whole-muscle cuts are safe at lower internal temps (rare is fine). Ground beef must reach 160°F (71°C).

pork.name: Pork

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.duration: 3–5 days fresh; up to 6 months frozen (cured products keep far longer)
storage.notes: USDA revised pork's safe internal temp to 63°C (145°F) in 2011 — pink, juicy pork loin is safe and preferred.

pork.description: Meat from domesticated pig (*Sus scrofa domesticus*), the world's most widely consumed meat by tonnage. Ranges from delicate, clean-flavored loin chops through forgiving, collagen-rich shoulder (ideal for braises and pulled pork) to the transformative fat-and-muscle combinations of belly. Heritage breeds (Berkshire, Mangalitsa, Iberico) produce fat with a higher melting point and deeper flavor than modern commodity pigs bred for leanness. Nearly every culture has a preserved-pork tradition: prosciutto, jamón, chorizo, bacon, guanciale, lardo.

loin.name: Loin (Chops, Roast)
loin.characteristics: Lean, mild, tender; chops are cut from the rack; roasts from the center-cut loin.
loin.uses: Quick pan-searing, roasting; dries out if overcooked.

shoulder.name: Shoulder / Butt
shoulder.characteristics: Heavily marbled, full of connective tissue and intramuscular fat.
shoulder.uses: Pulled pork, carnitas, braises, ragù, sausage.

belly.name: Belly
belly.characteristics: Alternating layers of fat and lean; becomes bacon when cured and smoked.
belly.uses: Roast whole, braise, cure for bacon/pancetta, slow-cook for pork belly bao.

tenderloin.name: Tenderloin
tenderloin.characteristics: Small, extremely tender, very lean cut running along the backbone.

ribs.name: Ribs (Baby Back, Spare, St. Louis)
ribs.characteristics: Meaty cuts from the rib cage, varying in meatiness and fat.

iberico.name: Iberico
iberico.characteristics: Spanish black pig fed acorns, producing deep crimson flesh and nutty fat.
iberico.uses: Cure for jamón; sear secreto and presa cuts quickly.

flavorProfile.notes: Pork fat caramelizes spectacularly — the basis for crackling, lardons, guanciale, bacon.

preparationTips: Brine loin and chops — they're so lean they have almost no margin for error.
Score skin in a tight grid for crackling; dry completely before roasting.
Shoulder is done when a fork twists freely in the meat — time ranges wildly by cut size.
Ribs are ready when the bones twist loose but the meat doesn't fall off — overcooked ribs disappoint.

composition.fdcDescription: Pork, fresh, loin, center rib (roasts), bone-in, separable lean and fat, cooked, roasted

fresh.storage: Sealed on a tray, bottom shelf (≤2°C).
tips: Bring chops to room temperature before searing.
Pat skin bone-dry for crackling.
Don't skip salting: pork breast and belly especially benefit from overnight dry brine.

safetyThresholds.notes: Ground pork to 160°F (71°C). Cured, shelf-stable products (jamón, prosciutto) are eaten raw.

lamb.name: Lamb

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

lamb.description: Meat from young domestic sheep (*Ovis aries*) under one year old (mutton is older animal, stronger flavored). Carries a distinctive grassy, slightly gamey flavor derived from branched-chain fatty acids in the fat — the very quality that makes it divisive. Milk-fed lamb (abbacchio) is palest and most delicate; spring lamb is the traditional Mediterranean Easter centerpiece; grass-finished lamb from New Zealand, Iceland, and Wales is intensely flavored and at its best with minimal fuss.

rack.name: Rack of Lamb
rack.characteristics: Eight cutlets from the rib primal, trimmed 'French' style with bones exposed.
rack.uses: Crown roast, roast whole, broil under a mustard-herb crust.

leg.name: Leg
leg.characteristics: Bone-in or butterflied; the Easter centerpiece of Mediterranean cuisine.

shoulder.name: Shoulder
shoulder.characteristics: Collagen-rich working muscle, heavily marbled, deeply flavored.

loin_chops.name: Loin Chops
loin_chops.characteristics: Small, tender T-bone-like chops from the lumbar region.

ground.name: Ground
ground.uses: Kofta, kibbeh, Greek moussaka, lamb burgers, meatballs.

shank.name: Shank
shank.characteristics: Heavily sinewy, collagen-packed lower leg joint.

flavorProfile.notes: Much of the distinctive flavor is in the fat — trim heavily or leave it, but don't meet in the middle.

preparationTips: Best served medium-rare (57°C/135°F) for tender cuts; braise cuts to pull-apart tender.
Stud legs and shoulders with slivers of garlic and rosemary before roasting.
Mint, preserved lemon, pomegranate — lamb loves sharp/acidic counterpoints.
Render mutton fat low and slow (suet) — it fries potatoes beautifully.

toAvoid: mild fresh cheeses with ground lamb

fresh.storage: Sealed on a tray, bottom shelf (≤2°C).
tips: Remove from fridge 45 min before cooking for even heating.
Score the fat cap on roasts to let fat render freely.
Serve on warm plates — lamb fat sets quickly and congeals on cold ones.

safetyThresholds.notes: Whole-muscle lamb is safe rare. Ground lamb to 160°F (71°C).

veal.name: Veal

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.container: Sealed on a tray, bottom shelf

veal.description: Meat from young cattle, typically 16–24 weeks old, with pale pink flesh and a delicate, mild flavor between chicken and beef. Rose veal (raised on a mixed diet with outdoor access) has replaced much of the ethically fraught formula-fed 'milk-fed' veal in modern European and North American markets. The gelatin-rich bones and shanks are the basis for classical French demi-glace and Italian osso buco.

chop.name: Veal Chop
chop.characteristics: Tender rib or loin chop with a mild flavor.

shank.name: Shank (Ossobuco)
shank.characteristics: Cross-cut hind shank with a marrow-filled bone center.
shank.uses: Ossobuco — the Milanese classic with gremolata and saffron risotto.

scallops.name: Scallopini / Scaloppine
scallops.characteristics: Thin slices pounded to even thickness.

flavorProfile.notes: Less assertive than beef; excellent carrier for sauces and aromatics.

preparationTips: Pound scallopini to even 3–4mm thickness for quick sear.
Don't overcook — veal dries out faster than beef.
Shanks for ossobuco should simmer 1.5–2 hours, barely breaking.
Roast veal bones deep brown before stock-making for flavor and color.

venison.name: Venison

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.duration: 3 days fresh; up to 12 months frozen
storage.notes: Wild-harvested venison should be aged 5–14 days at 1–3°C before butchering for tenderness.

venison.description: Meat from deer (typically *Odocoileus* species in North America and *Cervus elaphus* red deer in Europe). Extremely lean, iron-rich, and deeply flavored — gamier than any farmed red meat. Farmed venison is milder and more consistent; wild venison reflects the animal's diet and season. The leanness demands careful cooking: cook hot and fast to medium-rare, or slow-braise tough cuts with added fat.

flavorProfile.notes: Pairs famously with fruits, juniper, and cocoa — counterpoints that cut through the gaminess.

preparationTips: Always add fat: wrap loin in bacon or lardo; blend ground venison with pork fat.
Marinate tougher cuts in red wine and juniper for 12–24 hours.
Pull off heat 5°C before target — residual heat climbs fast in lean cuts.
Season aggressively — the flavor carries salt and pepper better than most meats.
doneness: medium-rare (57°C/135°F) only — anything further dries out badly

safetyThresholds.notes: Ground venison to 160°F (71°C). Wild game may carry chronic wasting risk in some regions — check local guidance.

chicken.name: Chicken

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.container: Sealed, on a rimmed tray on the bottom shelf
storage.duration: 1–2 days fresh; up to 9 months frozen
storage.notes: Never refreeze thawed raw chicken. Cook within 24h of thawing.

chicken.description: Domesticated fowl descended from the red junglefowl (*Gallus gallus domesticus*) of Southeast Asia. The world's most consumed protein, with an exceptionally mild, slightly sweet flesh that carries seasonings and sauces across virtually every global cuisine. White breast meat is lean and quick-cooking; dark thigh and leg meat is richer and forgiving under long heat. Select birds with plump, unblemished skin, pale flesh, and a clean smell; air-chilled or pasture-raised birds yield noticeably better flavor.

broiler.name: Broiler / Fryer
broiler.characteristics: Young, tender bird 7–10 weeks old, 2–5 pounds.
broiler.uses: Roasting, frying, grilling, sautéing — the default supermarket chicken.

roaster.name: Roasting Hen
roaster.characteristics: Older bird, 3–5 months, 5–7 pounds, with more fat and deeper flavor.
roaster.uses: Roasting whole or spatchcocked; richer stock.

heritage.name: Heritage Breed
heritage.characteristics: Slow-growing breeds like Bresse or Jersey Giant with firm, dense flesh.
heritage.uses: Traditional roasts, poule au pot, demands longer moist cooking.

poussin.name: Poussin
poussin.characteristics: Young bird under 4 weeks, 400–500g, extremely tender.

flavorProfile.notes: Takes on the character of its seasoning. Dark meat is richer and more forgiving than breast.

preparationTips: Dry-brine for 12–24h for crisp skin and seasoned flesh.
Temperature matters more than time: breast 63°C (145°F), thigh 74°C (165°F).
Rest whole birds 15 min before carving; joints 5 min.
Spatchcock to cook whole birds in half the time with more even browning.

composition.fdcDescription: Chicken, broilers or fryers, breast, meat only, cooked, roasted

toAvoid: very assertive blue cheeses on white meat

fresh.storage: Coldest part of fridge, ≤4°C, on a tray to catch drips.
tips: Remove giblets promptly.
Pat dry before seasoning — water is the enemy of crisp skin.

safetyThresholds.notes: USDA-mandated internal temperature at the thickest point, away from the bone.

turkey.name: Turkey

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.container: Original packaging or vacuum seal on a tray
storage.duration: 1–2 days fresh; up to 12 months frozen whole
storage.notes: A 14-lb bird takes ~3 days to thaw in the fridge. Never thaw on the counter.

turkey.description: Native North American fowl (*Meleagris gallopavo*) domesticated by Indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica and now raised worldwide. Leaner than chicken with a slightly gamier, more savory profile. Heritage breeds (Bourbon Red, Narragansett) offer deeper flavor than the commodity Broad-Breasted White. Whole birds are a centerpiece of fall and winter feasts; breast cuts and ground turkey serve as year-round lean protein staples.

broad_breasted_white.name: Broad-Breasted White
broad_breasted_white.characteristics: Commodity bird bred for rapid growth and large breast muscles.
broad_breasted_white.uses: Holiday roasts; benefits heavily from brining.

heritage.name: Heritage Breeds
heritage.characteristics: Bourbon Red, Narragansett, Standard Bronze — slower growth, more dark meat, deeper flavor.
heritage.uses: High-end roasts where flavor beats portion size.

wild.name: Wild Turkey
wild.characteristics: Foraged, lean, strongly flavored dark meat throughout.
wild.uses: Braising, smoking, confit; whole roasts are tough without care.

flavorProfile.notes: Leaner than chicken, so overcooked breast dries fast. Dark meat is genuinely flavorful.

preparationTips: Wet-brine 12–24h for moisture (1 cup kosher salt per gallon water).
Separate cooking of dark/white meat (spatchcock or parts) gives better results than a whole bird.
Pull breast at 63°C (145°F), rest to climb; thigh should reach 74°C (165°F).
Let rest 30+ minutes before carving — the temperature equalizes and juices reabsorb.

fresh.storage: Sealed, on the bottom shelf; allow 24h per 4–5 lbs to thaw frozen birds in the fridge.
tips: Remove giblets and neck from cavity.
Fully thawed before cooking — no exceptions for food safety.

safetyThresholds.notes: Insert thermometer into thickest part of the thigh, not touching bone.

duck.name: Duck

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.duration: 2 days fresh; up to 6 months frozen
storage.notes: Confit stored submerged in its own fat keeps 2–3 months refrigerated.

duck.description: Waterfowl (*Anas platyrhynchos domesticus*) prized across Chinese, French, and Southeast Asian traditions for its rich dark meat, thick insulating layer of subcutaneous fat, and legendary crisp skin. Pekin (Long Island) is the everyday breed; Muscovy and Moulard produce deeper flavor and the foie gras / magret of French cuisine. Every part has a use — the fat renders to a cooking medium rivaling olive oil, the carcass makes extraordinary stock, and the legs become confit.

pekin.name: Pekin (Long Island)
pekin.characteristics: White-feathered, milder flavor, pale flesh, thick fat cap; the standard American/Chinese duck.
pekin.uses: Whole roasts (Peking duck), crispy confit legs.

muscovy.name: Muscovy
muscovy.characteristics: Leaner, stronger flavor, firmer dark flesh; South American origin.

moulard.name: Moulard
moulard.characteristics: Pekin × Muscovy hybrid. Very large breasts ideal for foie gras or magret.

flavorProfile.notes: Pairs brilliantly with stone fruits and aromatic acid (orange, cherry, plum).

preparationTips: Score skin in a tight crosshatch through the fat layer but not the flesh.
Start breasts skin-side down in a cold dry pan to render fat gradually.
Reserve rendered fat — it's the best potato-roasting medium on earth.
Rest magret 8 min before slicing against the grain.

fresh.storage: Sealed on a tray, bottom shelf.
tips: Pat skin bone-dry; overnight uncovered in the fridge improves crispness.
Break down whole ducks into parts for faster, more even cooking.

safetyThresholds.notes: Breast meat is safely served medium-rare (57–60°C); legs must reach 74°C / 165°F.

goose.name: Goose

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.notes: A whole frozen goose needs 2–3 days to thaw in the fridge.

goose.description: Domesticated waterfowl (*Anser anser domesticus*) with exceptionally rich, dark, iron-heavy flesh and an extraordinary layer of fat that, when rendered, rivals duck fat for roasting potatoes and confiting. A traditional centerpiece of European winter feasts (Christmas goose in Germany, Britain, Scandinavia) whose popularity declined with industrial chicken and turkey but endures in heritage cooking.

flavorProfile.notes: Entire bird is dark meat — think of it as a very rich version of duck leg.

preparationTips: Prick the skin all over (not the flesh) to release fat during roasting.
Ladle off rendered fat every 30 min and reserve — you'll get a liter or more.
A whole goose serves fewer people than you'd expect for its weight (bony frame, lots of fat).

safetyThresholds.notes: All parts should reach 74°C (165°F) — no medium-rare goose.

quail.name: Quail

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.container: Sealed, flat in a single layer

quail.description: Small game bird (*Coturnix japonica* or *Colinus virginianus*) with dark, tender, mildly sweet flesh and a delicate, almost nutty flavor. Each bird serves one as an elegant appetizer or two as a component of a larger plate. Farmed quail are mild and consistent; wild quail carry a more pronounced gamey edge. Cook hot and fast — 10 minutes is often all they need.

flavorProfile.notes: Eat with hands — there's no dignified way to use cutlery.

preparationTips: Spatchcock for even cooking — they're too small to roast whole reliably.
10 minutes total at 230°C (450°F) is usually enough for spatchcocked birds.
Brush with a glaze (honey-soy, pomegranate molasses) during the last 2 min.

safetyThresholds.notes: Commercial quail is USDA-inspected; some chefs pull earlier on pristine farm product — proceed at your own risk.

atlantic_salmon.name: Salmon

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

tips: Keep in coldest part of refrigerator
Use within 24 hours of purchase for best flavor
Wrap in moisture-proof paper or plastic before freezing

atlantic_salmon.description: Oily cold-water fish (*Salmo salar*, Atlantic) prized for its rich orange flesh, generous omega-3 fats, and forgiving, flaky texture. Farmed salmon from Norway, Scotland, and Chile supplies most of the world market; wild Atlantic stocks are heavily restricted. Flavor ranges from buttery and mild (farmed) to deeply savory and almost meaty (wild). Essential in everything from Scandinavian cured gravlax to Japanese sushi, French en papillote, and American cedar-plank grilling.

preparation.notes: Leave skin on during cooking for easier handling and extra nutrients

healthBenefits: Heart health (reduces blood pressure and inflammation)
Brain function (enhances memory and cognitive performance)
Joint health (reduces stiffness and arthritis symptoms)
Bone health (contains vitamin D and phosphorus)
Mental well-being (omega-3s may help reduce depression symptoms)

pan_sear.timing: 4-5 minutes skin side, 2-3 minutes flesh side
pan_sear.notes: Start with very hot pan, cook skin side first until crispy

commonMistakes: Starting in a cold pan (causes sticking)

considerations: Look for ASC or MSC certification
Closed containment farming reduces environmental impact

flavorProfile.notes: Brown in dry heat for Maillard, then finish gently to stay tender.

preparationTips: Salt 40 min before cooking for well-seasoned result.
Rest after cooking to redistribute juices.

tuna.name: Tuna

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.notes: Thaw in refrigerator — never at room temperature.

tuna.description: Large, fast-swimming pelagic fish (*Thunnus spp.*) with dense, meaty red flesh, frequently compared to beef. Yellowfin (ahi) and bigeye are prized raw for sushi and sashimi; bluefin (the most prized and most endangered) delivers the fattest toro belly cuts; skipjack dominates canning. Sears beautifully with a rare center; overcooks quickly to chalky dryness. Buy only from sources rated Best Choice or Good Alternative by Seafood Watch — some populations are severely overfished.

preparation.notes: Can be eaten raw or cooked to desired doneness

flavorProfile.notes: Brown in dry heat for Maillard, then finish gently to stay tender.

preparationTips: Salt 40 min before cooking for well-seasoned result.
Rest after cooking to redistribute juices.

shrimp.name: Shrimp

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.notes: Thaw in refrigerator — never at room temperature.

shrimp.description: Small decapod crustaceans (*Penaeidae, Pandalidae*) harvested worldwide — the most consumed seafood in the United States. Sweet, briny flesh that turns from translucent grey-blue to opaque pink in seconds. Sold by count-per-pound (U-15 jumbo down to 61/70 small). Prawns are similar and often used interchangeably. Star in shrimp scampi, Thai tom yum, Spanish gambas al ajillo, Cajun étouffée, and Southeast Asian curries.

flavorProfile.notes: Brown in dry heat for Maillard, then finish gently to stay tender.

preparationTips: Salt 40 min before cooking for well-seasoned result.
Rest after cooking to redistribute juices.

cod.name: Cod

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
Enhanced flavor extraction

storage.notes: Thaw in refrigerator — never at room temperature.

cod.description: Lean, flaky white fish (*Gadus morhua* Atlantic, *G. macrocephalus* Pacific) with large, moist flakes and a mild, slightly sweet flavor. The fish that built global fisheries — cornerstone of British fish and chips, Portuguese bacalhau, Spanish brandada, and Scandinavian lutefisk. Overfishing collapsed Atlantic stocks in the 1990s; Pacific and Icelandic cod are now more sustainable alternatives. Rich in protein and B12, low in fat, takes any seasoning beautifully.

flavorProfile.notes: Brown in dry heat for Maillard, then finish gently to stay tender.

preparationTips: Salt 40 min before cooking for well-seasoned result.
Rest after cooking to redistribute juices.

halibut.name: Halibut

preparationTips: Best for subtle preparation methods
